\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

NER exhibits oracle scaling ($c{\approx}0.5$) but aggregation fails above $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$; entity construction and LP selection ($+0.3$\textendash$1.4$\,pp) bypass sample-level selection by operating at entity granularity rather than resolving the introspection boundary.
The fundamental barrier is not that agreement signals lack information, but that this information does not translate into discriminative power at the sample level: selection alignment $\alpha{\to}0$ even when quality correlation $\rho$ is substantial.
For small sample sizes (e.g., SQL $n{=}196$), absence of significant improvement may reflect insufficient power rather than true absence of effect.

Our evidence is correlational and theoretical (MBR framework, conditional decomposition), not interventional: we have not performed controlled interventions (e.g., artificially varying degeneracy while holding other factors constant), and the cascade stages interact in ways that resist decomposition into independent causal effects ($R^2{<}0$; \S\ref{sec:selection_gap}); causal claims require future intervention experiments.

Scope: structured IE (NER primary, RE and SQL exploratory), English only, open-weight (Qwen and LLaMA) and closed-source (GPT-5.5) families, fine-tuned (4B--14B) and zero-shot (72B, GPT-5.5) regimes, sample budget $N{\leq}32$.
Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; the RE extension covers a single SciERC benchmark ($n{=}207$ non-zero instances; 55.5\% yield zero F1 from upstream entity span errors rather than relation classification failure), and the SQL extension covers a single Spider subset ($n{=}196$) with 87.2\% degeneracy---both are exploratory and do not support generalization claims.
All experiments use English-language datasets; cross-lingual generalization remains untested.
Cross-model consistency results (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}) are limited to one dataset (Few-NERD) and one model pair (Qwen3-8B + LLaMA-3.1-8B).
Entity-level construction assumes the model produces useful partial outputs across samples; when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 51\% F1${=}0$), this precondition fails and construction cannot improve over greedy.
Entity-level construction requires $N{\times}$ inference cost for $+1$\textendash$1.4$\,pp gain; cost-effectiveness may not justify deployment in resource-constrained settings.
We cover 4B\textendash 14B fine-tuned, 72B zero-shot, and GPT-5.5 zero-shot; the gap persists across all but behavior with 72B fine-tuning is untested.
Frontier API models exhibit markedly different degeneracy profiles (e.g., Claude Sonnet~4 at 74\% vs.\ DeepSeek Chat at 5.5\%; Table~\ref{tab:frontier_sc_cross}), suggesting that our findings from fine-tuned open-weight models may not fully generalize to proprietary systems.
The 72B zero-shot comparison simultaneously varies model family (Qwen3$\to$Qwen2.5), training regime (fine-tuned$\to$zero-shot), and quantization (FP16$\to$AWQ 4-bit); these factors cannot be fully disentangled.
Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.
The hidden-state probe requires per-dataset training; leave-one-dataset-out AUROC drops to $0.559$\textendash$0.671$ (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}), limiting practical deployment without target-domain labeled data.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection); these confirm robustness on the key positive and negative datasets. SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), which reflects limited within-seed statistical power.
Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
4	These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
5	Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
6	The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
7	Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
8	This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for NER?
9	We investigate this question for NER and extend exploratorily to SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.
10	
11	The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
12	Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
13	This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
14	We show this assumption fails.
15	Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
16	Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
17	Our diagnostic framework addresses this question: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) characterize how strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.
18	
19	We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
20	Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC (all $p{\geq}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
21	Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.021$, selection family $k{=}21$).
22	To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated nine method categories spanning prompt-based self-verification, latent-space aggregation, and supervised classifiers (Table~\ref{tab:method_summary}).
23	No method produces statistically significant F1 improvement over majority vote on any tested configuration across three NER datasets and two model families (Appendix~\ref{app:method_coverage}).
24	A supervised hidden-state probe achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.63$\textendash$0.88$ from a single forward pass, exceeding prompt-based self-judgment (${=}0.51$) but not uniformly exceeding multi-sample agreement (${=}0.87$)---an introspection boundary modulated by task complexity (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

26	These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), 4B/14B ablations, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.

This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
We show this assumption fails.
Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
Our diagnostic framework addresses this question: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) characterize how strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC (all $p{\geq}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.021$, selection family $k{=}21$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated nine method categories spanning prompt-based self-verification, latent-space aggregation, and supervised classifiers (Table~\ref{tab:method_summary}).
No method produces statistically significant F1 improvement over majority vote on any tested configuration across three NER datasets and two model families (Appendix~\ref{app:method_coverage}).
A supervised hidden-state probe achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.63$\textendash$0.88$ from a single forward pass, exceeding prompt-based self-judgment (${=}0.51$) but not uniformly exceeding multi-sample agreement (${=}0.87$)---an introspection boundary modulated by task complexity (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), 4B/14B ablations, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
